title: Psychosocial pathways of etomidate misuse among Chinese youth in drug rehabilitation institutions
abstract: Background: Etomidate, an ultra-short-acting gamma-aminobutyric acid type A anesthetic, has been widely misused across East and Southeast Asia. By 2024, it became the most frequently misused anesthetic or psychotropic substance in China, with 86.4% of users younger than 35. Objective: This study explored how young people recruited from Chinese drug rehabilitation institutions initiated and sustained etomidate vaping, attempted to stop, and understood the psychosocial factors associated with continued use and return to use. Methods: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 103 participants (aged 15–35) with a history of etomidate misuse, recruited from drug rehabilitation institutions. Transcripts were analyzed using codebook-oriented thematic analysis. Results: Five themes concerned uninformed initiation, motivational pathways, device-related habituation, harms, and cessation attempts followed by returning to use. Nearly half were initially unaware that the product contained etomidate. A rapid, short-lived effect was described as promoting repeated inhalation, and negative emotion regulation was the most common motive for continued use. Device portability and concealability were associated with use across settings and everyday urges. Commonly self-reported harms included cognitive and motor difficulties, emotional changes, and hazardous driving. Cessation strategies included distraction, avoiding other users, and changing environments; however, online peer contact and drug-related digital content were described as re-evoking urges and contributing to return to use. Conclusion: Among young users in drug rehabilitation institutions in China, self-reported etomidate vaping experiences were characterized by limited risk awareness, emotion-regulation motives, device affordances, and digital social exposure. These findings suggested the potential value of emotion-regulation-focused interventions and platform-level governance.
